steps.observation: Write a short story about a lighthouse keeper.

steps.action:
# The Last Light

Every evening, Margaret climbed the 127 steps.

She had counted them so many times that the number lived in her bones, the way old songs do. Her knees ached on cold nights, but she never considered the elevator that the county had offered to install. The stairs were part of the ritual, and the ritual was the point.

She had inherited the lighthouse from her father, who had inherited it from his mother, who had simply shown up one winter and never left. The Calloway family had a talent for staying put.

The light itself was automated now. Had been for eleven years. The county kept Margaret on as caretaker — a polite word that meant she swept the floors, checked the machinery, and filed weekly reports that no one seemed to read. She understood that her real purpose was to justify the building's existence on the budget spreadsheet. A lighthouse with no keeper felt, to some people, like a lighthouse with no soul.

She didn't mind being a soul.

On clear nights she sat at the top with her logbook and wrote down what she saw. Ships she recognized by their silhouettes. Storm patterns she could read like handwriting. Occasionally a whale, a dark comma rising and sinking against the horizon.

Tonight the fog had come in thick, and she could barely see the water below. The light swept through it anyway, patient and indifferent, the way she imagined God might be if God existed and had a reasonable job.

A knock came at the door at the base of the tower. She was not expecting anyone.

The boy was perhaps sixteen, soaking wet, his bicycle leaning against the rocks behind him. He looked embarrassed to be there.

"I got turned around," he said. "In the fog. I know it sounds stupid."

"It doesn't," she said, and meant it. "Come in."

She made tea on the small stove and let him sit by the window until some color returned to his face. He looked at everything with the careful eyes of someone who wanted to remember it. She recognized that. She had looked at this place the same way when she was young, before the looking became breathing.

"Does it get lonely?" he asked, the way everyone eventually asked.

She thought about it honestly, the way she always tried to.

"It gets quiet," she said. "Those aren't the same thing."

He seemed to turn that over in his mind. Outside, the light kept moving — not searching, she always thought, but *offering*. There was a difference. You couldn't make anyone see it. You could only keep it burning and trust that the people who needed it were out there in the dark, looking.

The boy finished his tea. The fog had thinned enough to see the road.

"Thank you," he said at the door.

"127 steps to the top," she said, "if you ever want to see it properly. Come back on a clear night."

She watched his bike light wobble down the road and disappear. Then she climbed back up. Her knees ached. The light turned and turned, indifferent to whether anyone was watching, faithful anyway.

That, she had always thought, was the whole lesson.
